one_liner: WebAssembly port of TweetNaCl Ed25519 sign/verify for browsers, Node and Deno; ~4-6x faster than tweetnacl-js warmed up.
what_it_does: It provides Ed25519 key generation, detached signing and verification for JavaScript runtimes. The code is hand-written WAT compiled to a Wasm blob that is embedded as base64 in an ES module. There are five exports (sign, verify, newKeyPair, keyPairFromSeed, keyPairFromSecretKey) that mirror tweetnacl-js's nacl.sign.detached family and use the same Uint8Array key and signature formats. It is not a drop-in replacement: every function returns a Promise, only detached signatures exist, and there is no nacl object, no low-level crypto_sign API and no constants. SHA-512 and randomness come from the platform: crypto.subtle / getRandomValues in browsers and Deno, and node:crypto in Node.
how_it_is_fast: It runs the same TweetNaCl algorithms: 16-limb radix-2^16 field elements mod 2^255-19, and a constant-time cswap double-and-add over extended twisted Edwards coordinates for both fixed-base and variable-base scalar multiplication, with no precomputed tables. The gain comes from moving limb arithmetic from tweetnacl-js's Float64Array math to Wasm i64 integer ops. The 16x16 schoolbook field multiply is fully unrolled, which the source calls 'the hottest path of the entire library'. SHA-512 is delegated to the native Web Crypto or Node implementation instead of JS, which widens the gap on long messages. Shipping precompiled Wasm avoids JIT warm-up, hence the large first-call ratios.
when_to_use: You use tweetnacl-js only for Ed25519 signatures and must support runtimes without native Web Crypto Ed25519 (Chrome before 137, Firefox before 129, Safari before 17)
Cold-start-sensitive pages that sign or verify once right after load (e.g. an auth token): the README shows first-call sign/verify of 1.3-3 ms vs 8-44 ms for tweetnacl-js
Verifying signatures over large payloads (tens of KB) in the browser, where native SHA-512 helps: ~5.6-5.9x vs tweetnacl-js on an ~80 KB message
Bundle-size-sensitive front ends that need only signing: 7.4 kB min+gz vs 10.6 kB for tweetnacl-js (which also includes box/secretbox)
You want TweetNaCl's constant-time design (no secret-dependent branches or memory access), not the BigInt field arithmetic of noble-ed25519 v1
when_not_to_use: Modern targets with native Web Crypto Ed25519 sign/verify (Chrome 137+, Firefox 129+, Safari 17+, Node 16.17+, Deno 1.26+); watsign was never benchmarked against these native paths
Strict-CSP pages or Chrome MV3 extensions: the watever-js-wrapper glue calls indirect eval on the JS import strings, and issue #4 (open) reports it failing in MV3
Synchronous code paths, X25519/box/secretbox, batch verification or other curves: none are provided
Choosing between it and today's @noble/ed25519 (3.2.0): the noble comparison used noble-ed25519 1.2.6 from 2021, so the '1.2-3x faster than noble' claim is outdated

Consensus-critical or compliance-driven use: there is one maintainer, the project has been stale since 2024-04, it has no audit, it gets ~154 npm downloads/month, and verification inherits TweetNaCl's non-strict rules

integration.form: module (ESM-only npm package; Wasm embedded as base64 in the JS; Deno can import mod.js from raw.githubusercontent.com or use npm:watsign)
integration.dependencies: watever-js-wrapper ^0.3.2 at runtime, plus the platform's Web Crypto (crypto.subtle SHA-512, getRandomValues) or node:crypto
integration.min_toolchain: Node >= 16 (package engines); ESM ('type': 'module'); browsers need WebAssembly and Web Crypto SHA-512; rebuilding needs the author's watever WAT bundler (0.5.2)
integration.platforms: Any JS runtime with WebAssembly: modern browsers, Node >= 16, Deno
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. There is one Wasm instance per imported module copy, and concurrent async calls interleave on its linear memory through watever's keep/free allocator; each worker loads its own copy.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — keys and signatures are byte-compatible with tweetnacl-js nacl.sign.detached (the tests check identical signatures), but every call is async, the names differ (sign = nacl.sign.detached), and only the high-level detached-signing API exists

gotchas: sign() does not check the secret-key length: the 64-byte check exists only as a comment in sign.wat. Passing the wrong value (e.g. the whole key pair) gives 'RuntimeError: memory access out of bounds' (issue #3) instead of tweetnacl's 'bad secret key size'. verify and the keyPair functions do validate sizes.

verify ports TweetNaCl's check (unpack A, reduce H, compute [H](-A) + [S]B, compare with R) without rejecting non-canonical S >= L, so it is not a strict RFC 8032 verifier and accepts malleated signatures just as tweetnacl-js does.

Tests only cover two fixed identities cross-checked against tweetnacl-js; there are no RFC 8032 or Wycheproof vectors. Version 0.1.6 fixed a byte-widening bug in i8_to_i64 that had corrupted the hash reduction, so avoid anything older than 0.1.6 (latest is 0.1.9).
Timing uses performance.now() around awaited calls, so the async hop through the Web Crypto promise is included; cold-start numbers are single samples that the README itself says vary between runs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings (ENG25519 AVX-512IFMA, SUPERCOP amd64-64-24k Ed25519, libsecp256k1, UltrafastSecp256k1) are native C or assembly and cannot run inside a browser or Deno sandbox. Pick watsign only when Ed25519 must run in JS or Wasm; on servers, use those native libraries or the runtime's built-in crypto.
verified_claims_summary: Setup: Intel i7-10700, Chromium 93 driven by puppeteer 10.4.0 via chrode 0.3.3, mean of 50 runs after 50 warm-ups, in October 2021. watsign signed and verified a 10-byte message in 0.67/1.11 ms and an ~80 KB message in 0.96/1.28 ms. tweetnacl-js 1.0.3 took 2.86/5.65 and 5.70/7.21 ms (4.3-5.9x slower) and noble-ed25519 1.2.6 took 1.00/3.09 and 1.27/3.24 ms (1.3-2.8x slower). The '33x' and '17x' cold-start figures are single first-call samples (tweetnacl sign of the long message at 43.88 ms vs 1.32 ms; noble short sign at 53.17 ms vs 2.99 ms).
status_note: Stale: the WAT core last changed in October 2021 (v0.1.6), and the latest release, v0.1.9 (2024-04-15), only fixed TypeScript exports. Two issues are open, including the CSP/MV3 breakage. It is MIT-licensed and small, but edits require the author's watever toolchain, and native Web Crypto Ed25519 now covers most of its use case.
